bodies.example: Consider a gifted teacher or artist pressured into finance who performs poorly and feels trapped.

prompt: Educational institutions have a responsibility to dissuade students from pursuing fields of study in which they are unlikely to succeed.
thesis: I agree that schools should advise students honestly, but I believe a duty to dissuade them would do more harm than good.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why honest advice is good
bodies.topic: First, schools do have a duty to give students honest and realistic advice.
bodies.example: For example, a counsellor who gently shares the true difficulty of a field helps a student plan wisely.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why dissuading is wrong
bodies.topic: Second, however, an active duty to dissuade students would often be mistaken and harmful.
bodies.example: Consider the many famous achievers who were once judged hopeless by their own teachers.

prompt: Some people believe that competition for high grades motivates students to excel in the classroom. Others believe that such competition seriously limits the quality of real learning.
thesis: I believe both views hold truth, though I lean toward the idea that moderate competition helps while excessive competition harms.

bodies.role: Body 1 — How competition motivates
bodies.topic: First, a healthy level of competition genuinely motivates students to do their best.
bodies.example: For example, a student may prepare more carefully simply to match the strong results of her classmates.

bodies.role: Body 2 — How excess harms learning
bodies.topic: Second, however, too much competition for grades can seriously damage real learning.
bodies.example: Consider a student who crams facts for a test, passes it, and forgets everything a week later.

prompt: Claim: Major policy decisions should always be left to politicians and other government experts. Reason: Politicians and other government experts are more informed and thus have better judgment and perspective than do members of the general public.
thesis: I agree that experts have valuable knowledge, but I disagree that major decisions should always be left to them alone.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why expert knowledge matters
bodies.topic: First, there is real truth in the reason that experts are better informed.
bodies.example: For example, an economist may understand the likely effects of a tax far better than the average voter.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why the public must have a say
bodies.topic: Second, however, major decisions should not always be left to experts alone.
bodies.example: Consider a major decision about going to war, which changes countless lives and belongs to the whole nation.

prompt: Some people believe that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside the student's field of study. Others believe that universities should not force students to take any courses other than those that will help prepare them for jobs in their chosen fields.
thesis: I lean toward requiring some breadth, but I accept that job preparation also deserves real weight.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why breadth matters
bodies.topic: First, studying outside one's field makes students wiser and more complete thinkers.
bodies.example: For example, an engineering student who studies ethics may use her skills more responsibly.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why job preparation matters
bodies.topic: Second, however, the opposing view rightly values courses that prepare students for work.
bodies.example: Consider a student deep in debt who urgently needs practical skills to find employment soon.

prompt: It is more harmful to compromise one's own beliefs than to adhere to them.
thesis: I agree that holding to our beliefs has real value, but I do not believe compromise is always the more harmful choice.

bodies.role: Body 1 — The value of holding to beliefs
bodies.topic: First, staying true to our beliefs is often genuinely important.
bodies.example: For example, a worker who refuses to lie even under pressure keeps both honour and a clear conscience.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why rigid adherence can harm
bodies.topic: Second, however, refusing ever to compromise can be just as harmful, if not more so.
bodies.example: Consider a leader so devoted to a failed idea that she refuses to change while her people suffer.

prompt: Claim: Colleges and universities should specify all required courses and eliminate elective courses in order to provide clear guidance for students. Reason: College students — like people in general — prefer to follow directions rather than make their own decisions.
thesis: I agree that clear guidance helps students, but I disagree that electives should be eliminated, and I doubt the reason behind the claim.

bodies.role: Body 1 — The value of clear guidance
bodies.topic: First, there is some value in giving students clear guidance about what to study.
bodies.example: For example, requiring basic writing and reasoning helps students in almost any later field.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why electives should stay
bodies.topic: Second, however, eliminating electives entirely would be a serious mistake.
bodies.example: Consider a student who finds her future career only because an elective sparked a new passion.

prompt: No field of study can advance significantly unless it incorporates knowledge and experience from outside that field.
thesis: I agree that outside knowledge often drives progress, but I believe the word no makes the claim too absolute.

bodies.role: Body 1 — How outside knowledge drives progress
bodies.topic: First, borrowing knowledge from other fields often leads to major advances.
bodies.example: For example, biology advanced enormously once it began using the methods of chemistry and physics.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why 'no field' is too absolute
bodies.topic: Second, however, the claim that no field can advance without outside knowledge goes too far.
bodies.example: Consider a mathematician who solves a long-standing problem using only the tools of mathematics itself.

prompt: True success can be measured primarily in terms of the goals one sets for oneself.
thesis: I agree that personal goals are an important measure of success, but I do not believe they are the only or primary one.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why personal goals matter
bodies.topic: First, measuring success by our own goals is genuinely meaningful.
bodies.example: For example, someone who dreams of being a caring parent may feel deeply successful without any fame.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why they are not the only measure
bodies.topic: Second, however, success cannot be measured only by the goals we set ourselves.
bodies.example: Consider someone whose only goal is to avoid all effort, which she easily achieves by doing nothing.

prompt: The general welfare of a nation's people is a better indication of that nation's greatness than are the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists.
thesis: I largely agree with this claim, though I believe achievements still contribute to a nation's greatness.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why welfare is the better indicator
bodies.topic: First, the general welfare of the people is indeed a better indicator of greatness.
bodies.example: For example, a country with brilliant scientists but hungry citizens has failed its most basic duty.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why achievements contribute too
bodies.topic: Second, however, achievements should not be dismissed as a sign of greatness.
bodies.example: Consider how medical discoveries lengthen lives or how great art enriches an entire culture.

prompt: The best test of an argument is the argument's ability to convince someone with an opposing viewpoint.
thesis: I agree that persuading an opponent is a strong test, but I do not believe it is the only measure of a good argument.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why persuading opponents is a strong test
bodies.topic: First, convincing someone who disagrees is indeed a powerful test of an argument.
bodies.example: For example, a lawyer who changes the mind of a doubting jury has clearly made a compelling case.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why it is not the only test
bodies.topic: Second, however, the power to convince is not the only mark of a good argument.
bodies.example: Consider a sound scientific argument that a person rejects simply because it offends her beliefs.

prompt: Nations should pass laws to preserve any remaining wilderness areas in their natural state.
thesis: I strongly support protecting wilderness, but I believe a law covering every remaining area would be too rigid.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why preserving wilderness is vital
bodies.topic: First, protecting wilderness through law brings deep and lasting benefits.
bodies.example: For example, protected forests clean our air and water and guard plants found nowhere else.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why 'any remaining' is too rigid
bodies.topic: Second, however, a law protecting every remaining wild area would be too rigid to be fair.
bodies.example: Consider a poor region that needs a small part of its wild land for water, food, or shelter.

prompt: In any field — business, politics, education, government — those in power should be required to step down after five years.
thesis: I agree that limiting time in power can be healthy, but I believe a fixed five-year rule for everyone would also cause harm.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why limits prevent abuse
bodies.topic: First, requiring leaders to step down can prevent the abuse that long power invites.
bodies.example: For example, officials who hold power for decades often become corrupt and hard to remove.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why a fixed rule is too rigid
bodies.topic: Second, however, forcing everyone out after exactly five years would be too rigid.
bodies.example: Consider a skilled leader removed just as she has finally mastered a difficult job.

prompt: Some people claim that the goal of politics should be the pursuit of an ideal. Others argue that the goal should be finding common ground and reaching reasonable consensus.
thesis: I lean toward seeking consensus, but I believe ideals must still guide the search for it.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why consensus is the wiser goal
bodies.topic: First, finding common ground is often the only way to make government actually work.
bodies.example: For example, an important law usually passes only when opposing sides agree to give something up.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why ideals must still guide it
bodies.topic: Second, however, the pursuit of ideals should not be abandoned in the search for agreement.
bodies.example: Consider reformers who refused to compromise on justice and changed unfair laws most people once accepted.

prompt: The best way to solve environmental problems caused by consumer-generated waste is for towns and cities to impose strict limits on the amount of trash they will accept from each household.
thesis: I agree that limiting waste can help, but I do not believe strict limits alone are the best solution.

bodies.role: Body 1 — How limits help
bodies.topic: First, limiting household trash can genuinely reduce the waste a town produces.
bodies.example: For example, a household charged for extra bags will quickly learn to waste less and recycle more.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why limits alone are not enough
bodies.topic: Second, however, strict limits alone are far from the best way to solve the problem.
bodies.example: Consider a family that wants to waste less but has no recycling service to make it possible.

prompt: We learn our most valuable lessons in life from struggling with our limitations rather than from enjoying our successes.
thesis: I largely agree that struggle teaches deeply, but I believe our successes also offer valuable lessons.

bodies.role: Body 1 — How struggle teaches
bodies.topic: First, struggling with our limitations often teaches our deepest lessons.
bodies.example: For example, a student who fails an exam may finally learn how to study properly.

bodies.role: Body 2 — How successes teach too
bodies.topic: Second, however, our successes also teach valuable lessons of their own.
bodies.example: Consider an athlete who wins a race and learns exactly which training methods truly work.

prompt: Claim: While boredom is often expressed with a sense of self-satisfaction, it should really be a source of embarrassment. Reason: Boredom arises from a lack of imagination and self-motivation.
thesis: I agree that boredom sometimes reveals a dull mind, but I do not believe it is always something to be ashamed of.

bodies.role: Body 1 — When boredom reflects a dull mind
bodies.topic: First, there is real truth in the reason behind the claim.
bodies.example: For example, a curious child left alone with simple objects will happily invent endless games.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why boredom is not always shameful
bodies.topic: Second, however, boredom is not always a source of embarrassment.
bodies.example: Consider a worker forced to repeat the same meaningless task for hours on end.

prompt: Some people believe that the most important qualities of an effective teacher are understanding and empathy. Others believe that it is more important for teachers to be rigorous and demanding in their expectations for students.
thesis: I believe both qualities matter, and that the best teachers combine warmth with high expectations.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why empathy matters
bodies.topic: First, understanding and empathy are clearly vital qualities in a teacher.
bodies.example: For example, a patient teacher can give a frightened student the confidence to keep trying.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why rigour matters
bodies.topic: Second, however, being rigorous and demanding is just as important.
bodies.example: Consider a demanding teacher who pushes her class to attempt work they thought was beyond them.

prompt: Claim: Though often considered an objective pursuit, learning about the historical past requires creativity. Reason: Because we can never know the past directly, we must reconstruct it by imaginatively interpreting historical accounts, documents, and artifacts.
thesis: I largely agree that history requires creativity, though I believe it also demands careful discipline and evidence.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why history requires creativity
bodies.topic: First, the reason behind the claim is sound, since the past can never be known directly.
bodies.example: For example, a few old letters and ruins must be imaginatively pieced together into a picture of a lost world.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why history also needs discipline
bodies.topic: Second, however, history requires careful discipline as much as creativity.
bodies.example: Consider a scholar who invents an exciting story that the surviving facts simply do not support.

prompt: Claim: No act is done purely for the benefit of others. Reason: All actions — even those that seem to be done for other people — are based on self-interest.
thesis: I agree that self-interest drives much of what we do, but I disagree that no act is ever truly selfless.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why self-interest is powerful
bodies.topic: First, there is real truth in the reason that self-interest shapes many of our actions.
bodies.example: For example, a person may give to charity partly to feel proud or to look good to others.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why genuine selflessness exists
bodies.topic: Second, however, some acts truly are done purely for the benefit of others.
bodies.example: Consider a person who dies trying to save a drowning stranger she will never meet again.

prompt: To understand the most important characteristics of a society, one must study its major cities.
thesis: I agree that cities reveal a great deal, but I do not believe they show the whole character of a society.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why cities reveal much
bodies.topic: First, a society's major cities do reveal many of its most important features.
bodies.example: For example, a capital city often shows a country's wealth, power, and cultural energy at a glance.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why cities are not the whole
bodies.topic: Second, however, cities alone cannot reveal the whole character of a society.
bodies.example: Consider the villages and countryside where many people live and old customs survive.

prompt: Scandals are useful because they focus our attention on problems in ways that no speaker or reformer ever could.
thesis: I agree that scandals can expose real problems, but I do not believe they are a reliably useful way to do so.

bodies.role: Body 1 — How scandals expose problems
bodies.topic: First, scandals really can force public attention onto serious problems.
bodies.example: For example, a scandal about unsafe products can suddenly push a government to pass stronger laws.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why scandals are unreliable
bodies.topic: Second, however, scandals are an unreliable and often harmful way to highlight problems.
bodies.example: Consider how a scandal can ruin an innocent person's reputation before the facts are even clear.

prompt: Claim: Governments must ensure that their major cities receive the financial support they need in order to thrive. Reason: It is primarily in cities that a nation's cultural traditions are preserved and generated.
thesis: I agree that cities deserve support, but I doubt the reason and believe the rest of the nation needs funding too.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why cities deserve support
bodies.topic: First, major cities genuinely do need and deserve strong government support.
bodies.example: For example, a well-funded city can offer good transport, hospitals, and jobs to millions.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why the reason is doubtful
bodies.topic: Second, however, the reason that culture lives primarily in cities is doubtful.
bodies.example: Consider the folk songs, crafts, and customs that survive best far from any major city.

prompt: Some people believe that government funding of the arts is necessary to ensure that the arts can flourish and be available to all people. Others believe that government funding of the arts threatens the integrity of the arts.
thesis: I lean toward the view that funding is necessary, but I accept that it can endanger artistic integrity.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why funding helps the arts flourish
bodies.topic: First, government funding genuinely helps the arts flourish and reach everyone.
bodies.example: For example, free museums and funded theatres let poor families enjoy art they could not otherwise afford.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why funding can threaten integrity
bodies.topic: Second, however, the opposing view rightly warns that funding can threaten artistic integrity.
bodies.example: Consider an artist who softens her honest message for fear of losing her public funding.

prompt: Claim: In any field — business, politics, education, government — those in power should step down after five years. Reason: The surest path to success for any enterprise is revitalization through new leadership.
thesis: I agree that fresh leadership often helps, but I believe a strict five-year rule and its reason both go too far.

bodies.role: Body 1 — How new leadership can revitalise
bodies.topic: First, there is real truth in the reason that new leadership can revitalise an enterprise.
bodies.example: For example, a struggling company can be transformed when a bold new leader takes charge.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why a rigid rule loses experience
bodies.topic: Second, however, forcing everyone out after five years would also do real harm.
bodies.example: Consider a skilled leader removed by the rule just as her long plans were starting to succeed.

prompt: In any field of endeavor, it is impossible to make a significant contribution without first being strongly influenced by past achievements within that field.
thesis: I largely agree that the past shapes new work, but I believe the word impossible claims too much.

bodies.role: Body 1 — How the past shapes new work
bodies.topic: First, past achievements really do shape almost every important contribution.
bodies.example: For example, a scientist must understand existing theories before she can improve upon them.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why 'impossible' is too absolute
bodies.topic: Second, however, the claim that contribution is impossible without such influence goes too far.
bodies.example: Consider a self-taught inventor who solves a problem in a way no expert had ever considered.

prompt: Nations should pass laws to preserve any remaining wilderness areas in their natural state, even if these areas could be developed for economic gain.
thesis: I strongly support protecting wilderness, but I believe a law covering every remaining area would be too rigid.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why preserving wilderness is vital
bodies.topic: First, protecting wilderness by law brings deep and lasting benefits.
bodies.example: For example, protected forests clean our air and water and guard plants found nowhere else.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why an absolute rule is too rigid
bodies.topic: Second, however, a law protecting every remaining area would be too rigid to be fair.
bodies.example: Consider a poor community whose only path out of poverty runs through a small part of its wild land.

prompt: Governments should offer a free university education to any student who has been admitted to a university but who cannot afford the tuition.
thesis: I largely support this policy, though I believe it must be funded and managed with care.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why need-based free tuition is worthwhile
bodies.topic: First, paying for admitted students who cannot afford tuition is plainly worthwhile.
bodies.example: For example, a gifted student from a poor family could become a doctor the whole society needs.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why it must be funded with care
bodies.topic: Second, however, the policy must be funded and managed carefully to work well.
bodies.example: Consider a government that promises free education but cannot afford it, leaving universities underfunded.

prompt: Claim: In any situation, the best way to persuade other people is to present them with facts and statistics rather than with emotional arguments. Reason: Facts are objective, so they are more persuasive than subjective appeals.
thesis: I agree that facts matter greatly, but I disagree that they are always more persuasive than emotion.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why facts persuade
bodies.topic: First, facts and statistics are indeed powerful tools of persuasion.
bodies.example: For example, clear data showing that a medicine works can convince doubtful patients to take it.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why emotion persuades too
bodies.topic: Second, however, facts alone are often not the most persuasive approach.
bodies.example: Consider how a single human story can stir more action than a page of statistics.

prompt: Some people believe that success in creative fields, such as painting, fiction writing, and filmmaking, primarily requires hard work and perseverance. Others believe that such success mainly requires innate talents that cannot be learned.
thesis: I believe both matter, though I lean toward the view that hard work plays the larger role.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why hard work matters most
bodies.topic: First, hard work and perseverance are essential to creative success.
bodies.example: For example, famous writers often rewrite their work many times before it is any good.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why talent matters too
bodies.topic: Second, however, the opposing view rightly notes that inborn talent also matters.
bodies.example: Consider a child who plays beautiful music almost effortlessly while others struggle for years.

prompt: In business, education, and government, it is always appropriate to remain skeptical of new leaders until those leaders show that they are worthy of trust.
thesis: I agree that healthy caution is wise, but I believe the word always makes the claim too strict.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why skepticism is wise
bodies.topic: First, a reasonable skepticism toward new leaders is usually wise.
bodies.example: For example, a new manager who vows great change should be judged by results, not words.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why 'always' goes too far
bodies.topic: Second, however, remaining skeptical in every case would be harmful.
bodies.example: Consider a team that refuses to cooperate with a capable new leader out of constant suspicion.

prompt: Claim: Group assignments that students must work together to complete should replace a substantial amount of traditional lecture-based instruction in college and university courses. Reason: It is vital for students to gain experience collaborating with peers to study a topic and to achieve a common goal.
thesis: I agree that collaboration is valuable, but I do not believe group work should replace a substantial part of lectures.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why collaboration is valuable
bodies.topic: First, the reason behind the claim is sound, since collaboration is a vital skill.
bodies.example: For example, a group project can teach teamwork that a silent lecture never could.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why lectures are still needed
bodies.topic: Second, however, group work should not replace a substantial amount of lecture teaching.
bodies.example: Consider a difficult subject that students cannot grasp until a skilled teacher explains it clearly first.

prompt: Some people believe that in order to be effective, political leaders must yield to public opinion and abandon principle for the sake of compromise. Others believe that the most essential quality of an effective leader is the ability to remain consistently committed to particular principles and objectives.
thesis: I lean toward the value of principle, but I believe some willingness to compromise is also necessary.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why principle matters most
bodies.topic: First, staying committed to principles is essential to truly effective leadership.
bodies.example: For example, great reformers changed the world by refusing to abandon their core beliefs.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why compromise is also needed
bodies.topic: Second, however, some willingness to compromise is also necessary in real leadership.
bodies.example: Consider a leader who must compromise on small points to pass a law that helps millions.

prompt: Formal education tends to restrain our minds and spirits rather than set them free.
thesis: I agree that poor schooling can restrain us, but I believe good education frees the mind far more than it limits it.

bodies.role: Body 1 — When education can restrain
bodies.topic: First, it is true that formal education can sometimes restrain the mind.
bodies.example: For example, a rigid classroom may punish the very questions that real thinking requires.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why good education frees the mind
bodies.topic: Second, however, good education frees the mind far more than it restrains it.
bodies.example: Consider a student who, through learning, can suddenly understand and judge the wider world.

prompt: The well-being of a society is enhanced when many of its people question authority.
thesis: I largely agree that questioning authority helps a society, though unlimited questioning can also do harm.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why questioning needs limits
bodies.topic: Second, however, questioning authority without limit can also harm a society.
bodies.example: Consider a society where no one trusts the police, the courts, or any shared law.

prompt: Governments should focus on solving the immediate problems of today rather than on trying to solve the anticipated problems of the future.
thesis: I agree that urgent problems deserve attention, but I believe ignoring the future would be a serious mistake.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why immediate problems matter
bodies.topic: First, governments are right to give urgent present problems real attention.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why the future cannot be ignored

prompt: Some people believe that college students should consider only their own talents and interests when choosing a field of study. Others believe that college students should base their choice of a field of study on the availability of jobs in that field.
thesis: I believe both matter, and that the wisest choice weighs personal interest together with job prospects.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why talents and interests matter

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why job availability matters
bodies.topic: Second, however, the availability of jobs cannot simply be ignored.
bodies.example: Consider a graduate with a beloved degree but no job prospects, struggling for years under debt.

prompt: Laws should be flexible enough to take account of various circumstances, times, and places.
thesis: I largely agree that laws need flexibility, but I believe too much flexibility can also undermine fairness.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why flexibility makes laws just

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why too much flexibility harms
bodies.topic: Second, however, too much flexibility can make laws unfair and unpredictable.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why it can distract

prompt: Some people believe that traveling to and living in numerous places increases one's ability to relate and connect to other people. Others believe that this ability is better cultivated by living in one place and developing a deep understanding of that community.

bodies.role: Body 1 — How wide travel builds connection

bodies.role: Body 2 — How deep roots build connection

bodies.role: Body 2 — How devices can help connection

prompt: Claim: When one is making a decision, it is better to have a limited number of options. Reason: The more options a person has, the more difficult it is to make a rational decision.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why limited options help

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why too few options harm
bodies.topic: Second, however, having too few options can be just as harmful.
bodies.example: Consider a patient given only one treatment when a better one exists but is not offered.

prompt: Because people increasingly feel compelled to share their personal details online, the right to privacy is eroding.
thesis: I largely agree that privacy is under threat, but I believe it is not lost and can still be protected.

bodies.role: Body 1 — Why privacy is eroding
bodies.topic: First, it is true that constant online sharing is weakening privacy.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why privacy can still be protected
bodies.topic: Second, however, the right to privacy is not lost and can still be defended.

prompt: Some people believe that journalism should make news entertaining to keep the public engaged and informed. Others believe that this practice prioritizes entertainment and undermines the mission of journalism.

bodies.role: Body 2 — Why entertainment undermines the mission
